newsitem.title: USA: Potential jurors called in key Fla. tobacco case.
newsitem.headline: Potential jurors called in key Fla. tobacco case.

text.p: A Florida court has begun the process of selecting a jury for the trial of a widely watched class-action lawsuit in which airline flight attendants claim they were sickened by secondhand smoke on U.S. passenger jets.
Trial of the case, known as Broin v Philip Morris Cos Inc et al, is scheduled for June 2.
Nearly 250 potential jurors filled out questionnaires on Wednesday and Thursday, presiding Dade County Judge Robert Kaye said at a pretrial hearing.

Kaye said language was not proving to be a major problem -- a critical issue in Miami's Dade County, where Spanish is spoken in a majority of households. Of 240 potential jurors brought in to fill out the questionnaire, fewer than a dozen had said they were not literate in English.

Kaye said he had not decided on the makeup of the jury panel but suggested to lawyers that six jurors and 12 alternates be chosen. He said he was recommending the unusually large number because of past high-profile cases, including the O.J. Simpson murder trial, where the jury panel was whittled by illness and other circumstances along the way.
"I'm thinking of what happened in the (O.J.) Simpson case," he said. "I don't want to get into that situation."
Edward Moss, an attorney for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc, objected to the large number, saying it would create "an unmanageable situation."
"We magnify the problems with more jurors," he said.
The jury questionnaire asked potential jurors if they smoke, when they started, whether they tried to quit and other details of their smoking history.

They were also asked whether they believed secondhand smoke causes disease, whether cigarette companies should be responsible for damage caused by their product and whether smokers have a right to smoke in public places.

The tobacco companies also made a last-minute bid to strip the case, filed on behalf of an estimated 60,000 flight attendants who may have contracted illnesses while working on U.S.-based airlines, of class-action status.

In a petition filed on Wednesday, eight of the ten defendants named in the lawsuit asked Kaye to decertify the class because "the basic predicates that this court and the Third DCA (appeals court) relied on for class certification are false."

The industry argued that the plaintiffs, during pre-trial discovery, had found that it was impossible to answer the basic predicate question "What level of exposure to secondhand smoke causes disease?"
The plaintiffs had admitted, the industry argued, that there was no one level of exposure to secondhand smoke that causes any disease.
"The discovery in this case now demonstrates that it is impossible to continue this case as a class action," the petition said. A hearing on the issue was set for May 29.
The industry has contended since the case was filed six years ago that it should not be tried as a class action because the claimed illnesses are unique to each individual.

In a trial plan, Kaye ruled that the case will be divided into two parts, with common issues such as the causes of illness and the alleged liability of the tobacco companies to be tried in the first stage and individual claims to be heard in the second.
